candidates.source_name: Ephrem the Syrian / Commentary on Exodus
candidates.source_attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Exodus IV.3 (NPNF S2 V13, Gwynn/Schaff trans., Oxford 1898). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Exodus (c. 360 AD)

Moses' hand made leprous in the bosom and then restored is, for Ephrem, the sign of the Incarnation given before the fact: humanity has become diseased in its hidden parts, and the Lord places it within his own bosom to bring it forth healed. The same hand that becomes leprous becomes healing for the leprous — a foreshadowing of the Word's assumption of the very flesh he will cleanse.

candidates.source_name: Ephrem the Syrian / Commentary on Exodus
candidates.source_attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Exodus IV.5 (NPNF S2 V13, Gwynn/Schaff trans., Oxford 1898). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Exodus (c. 360 AD)

Water turned to blood at Moses' word is the sign of judgment; water turned to wine at Cana is the sign of joy. Ephrem reads the two miracles as a single canonical inclusio: the first prophet inverts the river to bring judgment on Egypt; the true Lord inverts the water-pots to bring gladness to the wedding. The Word who turned the Nile to blood for accusation turns the jars of purification into the wine of the new covenant.

candidates.source_name: Ephrem the Syrian / Commentary on Exodus
candidates.source_attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Exodus IV.20 (NPNF S2 V13, Gwynn/Schaff trans., Oxford 1898). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Exodus (c. 360 AD)

The hostile encounter at the lodging-place, where the Lord seems to seek Moses' life, Ephrem reads as a covenant-rupture answered by covenant-restoration: it is the failure to circumcise Moses' son that opens the breach, and Zipporah's prompt circumcision that closes it. The Tewahedo reading harmonizes the canonical witness with Jub 48:1-2, which names Mastema as the immediate agent; the divine permission and the demonic accusation work together to vindicate the covenant.

Moses' hand made leprous in the bosom and then restored is, for Ephrem, the sign of the Incarnation given before the fact: humanity has become diseased in its hidden parts, and the Lord places it within his own bosom to bring it forth healed. The same hand that becomes leprous becomes healing for the leprous — a foreshadowing of the Word's assumption of the very flesh he will cleanse.

Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Exodus (c. 360 AD)

Water turned to blood at Moses' word is the sign of judgment; water turned to wine at Cana is the sign of joy. Ephrem reads the two miracles as a single canonical inclusio: the first prophet inverts the river to bring judgment on Egypt; the true Lord inverts the water-pots to bring gladness to the wedding. The Word who turned the Nile to blood for accusation turns the jars of purification into the wine of the new covenant.

candidates.draft_body:
Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Exodus (c. 360 AD)

The hostile encounter at the lodging-place, where the Lord seems to seek Moses' life, Ephrem reads as a covenant-rupture answered by covenant-restoration: it is the failure to circumcise Moses' son that opens the breach, and Zipporah's prompt circumcision that closes it. The Tewahedo reading harmonizes the canonical witness with Jub 48:1-2, which names Mastema as the immediate agent; the divine permission and the demonic accusation work together to vindicate the covenant.
